claims.text: A controlled minor microalloying addition of a targeted element will improve glass-forming ability in a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy.
The microalloying addition will enhance the thermal stability of the alloy's amorphous state.
The addition will disrupt local short-range order and thereby suppress crystallization.
The initial phosphorus-containing alloy is a metastable amorphous material with moderate glass-forming ability and limited thermal stability.
A minor addition of a targeted element should be introduced during alloy processing.
The additive should be incorporated during rapid solidification, such as melt spinning.
The intervention is effective only within a narrow additive-concentration window.
The additive enhances short-range chemical ordering.
The additive increases atomic packing heterogeneity.
Enhanced short-range chemical ordering and packing heterogeneity hinder the atomic mobility required for crystallization.
The additive creates local compositional fluctuations.
Local compositional fluctuations raise the energy barrier for atomic rearrangements and consequently delay crystallization kinetics.
Relative to an identically processed alloy without the additive, the modified alloy will have a wider supercooled-liquid region.
Relative to an identically processed alloy without the additive, the modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature.
Excessive additive content or inappropriate cooling rates may cause phase separation or unwanted crystalline phases.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the intervention acts by disrupting local short-range order, whereas the structural mediator says it enhances short-range chemical ordering. These directions are inconsistent unless distinct kinds of order are explicitly distinguished.
